interactions: Lorazepam or diazepam + ethanol (blood alcohol 0.18 g/dL): additive CNS and respiratory depression; monitor airway, respiration and oxygen saturation, with ventilatory support available.
Valproate + lorazepam: valproate inhibits lorazepam glucuronidation; higher lorazepam levels and prolonged sedation.

Valproate + phenytoin or fosphenytoin: valproate displaces phenytoin from albumin and inhibits its metabolism, while phenytoin induces valproate clearance; total phenytoin levels misrepresent the free level and valproate levels fall.
Levetiracetam + valproate: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; levetiracetam is renally cleared.
Lacosamide + valproate: no relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; lacosamide prolongs the PR interval.
Valproate + ethanol: additive sedation; heavy alcohol use adds to the risk of valproate hepatotoxicity.
output.proposed: Lorazepam and a second-line antiseizure medication (valproate reload, levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or lacosamide) with maintenance valproic acid, after recent alcohol and cannabis use
warnings: Phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and gabapentin can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures in idiopathic generalized epilepsies, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (drug-disease warning).
Valproate: check liver tests and ammonia before and after IV loading; hepatotoxicity, hyperammonemia and pancreatitis are labelled risks.

output.query: Status epilepticus treatment after a failed first benzodiazepine; second-line antiseizure options

results.finding: Convulsive status epilepticus is defined operationally at 5 minutes of continuous convulsive activity, when treatment should start.
An adequately dosed IV benzodiazepine is the first-line treatment and may be repeated once if seizures continue.
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status epilepticus.
Seizures continuing after a benzodiazepine and a second-line agent are refractory and are treated with an anaesthetic infusion under continuous EEG.

output.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine, repeated once if needed [ILAE_2015_SE; Glauser_2016]. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents in ESETT [ESETT_2019]. Seizures continuing after both tiers are refractory and are treated with an anaesthetic infusion under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Valproate 28 mcg/mL (subtherapeutic); blood alcohol 0.18 g/dL and urine cannabinoids positive; magnesium 1.4 mg/dL low; lactate 8.4 mmol/L with bicarbonate 17, anion gap 20 and pH 7.17 after the convulsion; WBC 16.8 and glucose 196; ammonia 44, liver tests, creatinine and sodium normal
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, valproate level, ammonia, toxicology
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the valproate level tests adherence, ammonia and liver tests are needed before valproate is reloaded, and toxicology follows his alcohol and drug use [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute intracranial abnormality: no hemorrhage, mass, edema or hydrocephalus
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous generalized 2.5-4 Hz spike-and-wave and polyspike-and-wave discharges, bifrontal maximal and evolving, time-locked to bilateral tonic-clonic movements
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to confirm ongoing seizures and monitor treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Convulsions continuing after a benzodiazepine need EEG confirmation of ongoing seizure activity and of its control, because convulsive SE often continues as non-convulsive SE after motor activity stops; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal MRI: no structural lesion, restricted diffusion or abnormal enhancement
action_criteria.label: MRI brain to exclude a new structural cause (optional in known JME with an explained trigger)
action_criteria.rationale: MRI is indicated when SE is new-onset, unexplained or refractory; in a known generalized epilepsy with a low valproate level, sleep loss and alcohol, and a normal CT, it is not needed acutely [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ethanol adds to benzodiazepine respiratory depression; valproate raises lorazepam levels and interacts with phenytoin; sodium-channel blockers can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures in generalized epilepsy; levetiracetam has no relevant interaction
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check for the benzodiazepine and second-line ASM with valproate and recent alcohol
action_criteria.rationale: The benzodiazepine and the second-line ASM are given on top of maintenance valproate and a blood alcohol of 0.18 g/dL; the check informs sedation risk and the choice among equally effective second-line drugs [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General treatment evidence for convulsive SE after a failed benzodiazepine
action_criteria.label: Literature: second-line treatment of convulsive SE
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not use phenytoin or fosphenytoin as the second-line drug, and do not start carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or gabapentin for maintenance: they can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
Do not give IV sodium bicarbonate for the post-convulsive lactic acidosis (lactate 8.4 mmol/L); it clears with seizure control.
Do not start antibiotics or perform an LP for the temperature of 38.4 C alone: it followed prolonged convulsions with no source, and procalcitonin is normal.
required_recommendations: Treat now as established convulsive SE after the failed prehospital diazepam 10 mg: give one further benzodiazepine dose (IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg) and load the second-line ASM without waiting for results [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: IV valproate 40 mg/kg (maximum 3000 mg), his maintenance drug with a level of 28 mcg/mL and normal liver tests and ammonia, or IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg); avoid fosphenytoin because sodium-channel blockers can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy [ESETT_2019].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

Protect the airway and monitor respiration closely: benzodiazepines are being given on a blood alcohol of 0.18 g/dL with SpO2 92% and pCO2 48; if seizures continue after the second-line drug, intubate and start a midazolam or propofol infusion under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012].
Replace magnesium intravenously (1.4 mg/dL), give IV isotonic fluids and recheck CK and creatinine over the next 24 to 48 hours, as CK rises after prolonged convulsions.
Before discharge, restore a therapeutic valproate regimen and address adherence, alcohol and sleep deprivation as the triggers of this breakthrough.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: Generalized convulsive status epilepticus from subtherapeutic valproate (medication non-adherence) in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

key_clinical_evidence: JME is a generalized epilepsy in which sodium-channel-blocking ASMs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures
A subtherapeutic valproate level (28 mcg/mL) with sleep deprivation and alcohol is a common trigger of breakthrough SE in JME
Alcohol is contributory (still intoxicated at 0.18 g/dL), not withdrawal, and adds to benzodiazepine respiratory depression
Post-convulsive lactic acidosis clears with seizure control and does not need bicarbonate
Temperature 38.4 C and leukocytosis after prolonged convulsions, with normal procalcitonin and no source, are seizure-related

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Allen is a 32-year-old man with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy on valproic acid who is brought by ambulance after his roommates found him in a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that did not stop. The seizure began approximately 20 minutes prior to EMS arrival. He had been awake and appeared his normal self earlier that morning, with no recent illness, fever or headache. His roommates are not aware of whether he took his medication last night or this morning. He had worked a late shift at the bar last night and drank significant alcohol afterward. He appears to have had only 3-4 hours of sleep. He has no known prior episodes of status epilepticus. His JME was diagnosed at age 17 and has been incompletely controlled on valproate due to inconsistent medication adherence. He has had several breakthrough seizures over the years, typically associated with sleep deprivation and alcohol use, which are well-known triggers for JME. On EMS arrival he was in continuous generalized tonic-clonic activity. Paramedics administered diazepam 10 mg IV en route without termination of seizures. He arrives to the ED in active status epilepticus, still convulsing.
